Newly hatched Western reef heron chicks emerge from eggs incubated at a consistent thermal regime of 36 °C [T = 36 °C] over a development period lasting approximately 25 days [ab = approximately 25 days]. Upon emergence, these altricial nestlings exhibit a wet weight at birth of 22.19 grams [Wwb = 22.19 grams], a modest mass typical for the genus. Prior to hatching, the initial wet weight of the freshly laid egg has been recorded at 27.38 grams [Ww0 = 27.38 grams], a value closely matching the Avibase reference of 28 grams for this species. This relatively small egg mass, representing roughly six percent of the female's ultimate body size, underscores a life-history strategy that balances clutch volume against the energetic demands of incubation. The nestlings grow rapidly under constant biparental provisioning, transitioning through the pin-feathered stage before preparing for their first flight. This developmental trajectory is characteristic of ardeids, where chicks are entirely dependent on parental feeding during the early weeks post-hatch.

Under the elevated body temperatures typical of actively foraging adults in a tropical coastal environment, approximately 40.5 °C [T = 40.5 °C], fledglings achieve their first sustained flight at 28 days after hatching [tx = 28 days after hatching], marking a critical milestone in the transition from nestling to independent juvenile. This period of flight feather maturation is followed by the attainment of puberty, which occurs at 84 days after hatching [tp = 84 days after hatching] under the same thermal regime at a temperature of 40.5 °C [T = 40.5 °C]. The relatively rapid progression to sexual maturity, completed within roughly three months, facilitates early recruitment into the breeding population. Juveniles then disperse from natal territories, often along the extensive mangrove-lined coastlines of West Africa and the Red Sea. During this sub-adult phase, individuals continue refining their foraging techniques in shallow tidal waters, preying upon small fish and crustaceans. The physiological readiness to breed at 84 days contrasts with the deferred age at which most individuals actually secure a territory and engage in their first reproductive attempt.

First successful reproduction in Western reef herons typically occurs at one year after hatching, a timing quantified as 365 days [tR = 365 days] when measured under the active metabolic body temperature of 40.5 °C [T = 40.5 °C]. This delay of roughly nine months beyond the onset of puberty reflects the ecological constraints of territory acquisition, nest construction, and the attainment of sufficient foraging proficiency to support offspring. During this interval, immature birds develop their nuptial plumage and engage in courtship displays that reinforce pair bonds. The single annual reproductive cycle is a further indicator of the species' conservative life-history strategy, with each breeding pair typically producing just one clutch per year [F_R_i = one clutch per year], containing between 1 and 5 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = between 1 and 5 eggs per clutch]. These reproductive metrics, combined with the deferred first breeding, yield a relatively low annual reproductive output that is compensated for by extended parental care and high chick survival in stable coastal habitats.

Adult body mass exhibits pronounced sexual dimorphism in this heron species, reflecting divergent energetic investments between the sexes. Females attain a maximum adult wet weight of 483 grams [Wwi = 483 grams] under favorable coastal foraging conditions, while males, which are typically more active in territorial defense and courtship, reach a lower ultimate wet weight of 400 grams [Wwi = 400 grams]. This 83-gram difference, approximately seventeen percent of the female's mass, is consistent with patterns observed in other Egretta species where females are proportionally larger to accommodate the energetic costs of egg production. Body condition fluctuates seasonally based on prey availability and the demands of the breeding cycle, with individuals losing mass during the incubation and chick-rearing phases. Field measurements from the Gulf of Guinea indicate that peak body masses are recorded in the pre-breeding period, when adults accumulate reserves for the upcoming reproductive effort. These values align closely with specimen-based records from museum collections across the species' range.

Longevity records for the Western reef heron indicate a maximum documented lifespan of approximately 22.3 years [am = approximately 22.3 years] under natural field conditions at an active metabolic body temperature of 40.5 °C [T = 40.5 °C]. This extended lifespan, approaching a quarter-century for the oldest individuals, is notable among ardeids and underscores the species' capacity for repeated breeding attempts over a prolonged adult phase. Annual adult survival rates are high, likely exceeding 80 percent in undisturbed habitats, with natural mortality primarily resulting from predation by raptors, starvation during prey shortages, and coastal habitat degradation. The combination of a long lifespan, a delayed first reproduction at one year (1 year since birth) [tR = 1 year since birth], and a modest annual clutch size of 1 to 5 eggs [N_R_i = clutch size of 1 to 5 eggs] positions this heron as a classic K-selected strategist among coastal waterbirds at a temperature of 40.5 °C [T = 40.5 °C]. Senescence eventually leads to a gradual decline in foraging efficiency and reproductive output, with the oldest observed individuals showing diminished provisioning rates before their natural death.
